reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare group of B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders that secrete an incomplete, truncated immunoglobulin heavy chain with no associated light chain
Three main types are recognised by heavy chain isotype: alpha, gamma and mu
Alpha heavy chain disease is the commonest and typically presents as immunoproliferative small intestinal disease with malabsorption, diarrhoea and weight loss
Gamma heavy chain disease (Franklin disease) often causes lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and, characteristically, palatal or uvular oedema, and may associate with autoimmune disease
Mu heavy chain disease is rare and usually arises in the setting of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia with vacuolated plasma cells in the marrow
The abnormal protein is often difficult to detect by routine electrophoresis, so immunofixation and immunoselection techniques are needed
Alpha heavy chain disease is linked to Campylobacter jejuni infection, and early antibiotic therapy can induce remission at the lymphoma stage
reference.pathophysiology: Heavy chain diseases arise from clonal B cells or plasma cells that carry deletions or mutations in the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene, so that a structurally abnormal, truncated heavy chain is produced which cannot bind light chains and is secreted alone. Each isotype reflects a distinct clinical entity. In alpha heavy chain disease, chronic antigenic stimulation of gut-associated lymphoid tissue, associated with Campylobacter jejuni, is thought to drive a marginal zone lymphoproliferation of the small bowel, which explains why antibiotics can be effective early. Gamma and mu variants represent clonal lymphoplasmacytic proliferations with their own tissue distributions and disease associations.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple myeloma and other plasma cell neoplasms
Coeliac disease and other causes of malabsorption (for alpha type)
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation seeking a heavy chain without light chain
Immunoselection or specialised immunochemical techniques to confirm the isolated heavy chain
Small bowel biopsy and imaging for suspected alpha heavy chain disease
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with immunophenotyping
Lymph node biopsy where lymphadenopathy is present
Testing for associated infection or autoimmune disease
redFlags: Severe malabsorption with weight loss and nutritional failure
Airway compromise from palatal or pharyngeal oedema in gamma type
Transformation to an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies by type and stage; early alpha heavy chain disease may respond to antibiotics, whereas advanced lymphomatous or aggressive disease carries a poorer prognosis and requires lymphoma-directed therapy.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because the abnormal protein evades routine electrophoresis
Overlooking a treatable infective driver in alpha heavy chain disease
Mistaking malabsorption for coeliac disease without considering immunoproliferative small intestinal disease
Failing to recognise transformation to aggressive lymphoma
